elements.note: Modern Ethel began as a short form of names starting with Ethel-.
Source of the Ed- in Edward, Edmund, Edgar and Edith.
Usual source of English names ending in -bert, such as Cuthbert.
Gives the -win of names such as Edwin, Godwin and Oswin.
Bosworth-Toller also lists an older, now rejected, analysis of Alfred from eald + friþ.
A different sige meaning 'setting of the sun' exists, but the name element means victory.
Bosworth-Toller notes it occurs frequently in proper names; Cynehild survives inside the place-name Kenilworth.
The -fred of Wilfred is friþ, but the -fred of Alfred is rǣd 'counsel'.
The same word as Old Norse áss (the Æsir); as a separate word it survives mainly in names.
Godgifu is the Old English form of Godiva.
Ecgberht is the source of the later name Egbert.
Wynflæd's second part, flǣd, has an uncertain meaning, often given as 'beauty'.
Related to Old Norse björn 'bear', but in Old English it means a man or warrior.
Common in women's names; St Hild of Whitby gives the modern Hilda.
Not the same as weald 'forest', which is a separate place-name word.
Mostly in women's names; it gives the -dred of Mildred and lies behind Audrey.
Bosworth-Toller notes it occurs often as a part of proper names.
Usually read as god 'God', but in some names it may be gōd 'good'; the two are hard to tell apart in spelling.
The commonest English place-name element; it later gave the word 'town'.
Easily confused with hamm; early spellings are needed to tell them apart.

elements.meaning: land hemmed in by water or marsh; river-meadow
elements.note: Looks the same as hām in modern names such as Fulham.

elements.meaning: wood, woodland clearing; later pasture, meadow
dwelling, farm, dairy farm; trading settlement
elements.note: Borrowed early from Latin vicus.

elements.meaning: fortified place, fort; later a town
elements.note: -bury comes from byrig, the dative case of burh.
Borrowed from Latin castra 'camp'; usually marks a Roman site.

elements.meaning: open country, land without trees; later arable land

examples.name: Sheffield
examples.gloss: open land by the River Sheaf

elements.meaning: hill, natural rise in the ground

elements.note: Possibly borrowed from British (compare Welsh cwm); KEPN gives both views.
In early names it usually means dry ground in a marsh, not an island at sea.

elements.meaning: heel; sharply projecting piece of ground, spur of a hill
wood, often of a single kind of tree
place; place of assembly; holy place

elements.note: Do not confuse with græf 'pit, trench', which also gives -grave.

elements.meaning: harbour; also market town, or town gate
elements.note: Borrowed from Latin; the meaning (harbour, market, gate) depends on the place.

elements.meaning: head; end or source; projecting ground, small hill

elements.note: Used in southern England; a separate ōra means 'ore'.
